title: Method for Creating a Tissue Microarray-Capable Slide-Scanning Acquisition Device
author: Steven P. Nilsen

A DIY automated scanning microscope Page 8 of 30 Materials: EQUIPMENT. Microscope: the method is applicable to many different microscopes, including upright and inverted wide-field and confocal microscopes from many manufacturers. This system was developed using a Leica DM4000 fluorescent microscope. An advantage of this microscope is that it has a motorized filter turret that allows use of individual excitation and emission filters for each fluorochrome. It is possible to use a multi-bandpass dichroic and emission filter and individual excitation filters or light sources, e.g., lasers or LEDs. Our experience, however, is that these capture a greater degree of nonspecific signal from tissue autofluorescence, which is detected across a wide spectrum of excitation and emission wavelengths. Stage: a motorized stage is required. The system described is equipped with a Ludl BioPrecision2 xy stage with mounting accessories for the Leica DM4000. The stage was selected because of its high resolution (<0.5 µm repeatability) and linear encoders that allow precise positioning. The microscope is also equipped with a Ludl focus motor with linear encoder for z axis control. Both stage and focus motor are controlled by a Ludl MAC 6000. Specimen holder: the system described here is equipped with a Ludl 4 position slide holder (to allow 4 TMA slides to be imaged at once). Systems with single slide holders or, alternatively, automated high-capacity slide holders, can also be used. Care must be taken to ensure that slides are placed in register in the xz plane and are aligned with the camera focal plane with z variance of less than 30 µm across the slides. Objectives: these are infinitely customizable. This system is equipped with a Leica HC PL FLUOTAR 5x 0.15NA objective for preliminary scans and HC PL APO 20x 0.70NA objective for image acquisition. For intestinal tissue cores arranged in a microarray we found that a 20X objective provides the optimal combination of high resolution and manageable file size. Other objectives can be used, depending on the samples and goals. Filter cubes: care should be taken to ensure that the filter cubes adequately isolate fluorochromes without significant bleed-through between channels. The system described here is equipped with Chroma ET filter sets 49000, 49002, 49008, and 49009, e.g., for detection of Hoechst 33342, Alexafluor 488, Alexafluor 594, and Alexafluor 647, respectively. These filters are also suitable for imaging fluorochromes with similar excitation and emission wavelengths. The high-
throughput Modified Magnetron (ET) sputter-coated line of filters was selected for durability and long life. The filters were mounted in cubes for Leica DM series microscopes and aligned by the

(optional) If you want to create multi-channel image stacks of all the regions, then select Journal > Loop > Loop for all Images in Directory. Select the directory in which the images are saved and run the journal collect multiple wavelengths into stacks.JNL. v. (optional) Most virtual microscope applications, including OMERO, require a pyramidal image file. This can be created from the multi-wavelength image stack using the Python-based program Stitcher (Glencoe Software) with the pyramid option. b. Stitching with ASHLAR: i. ASHLAR is open source software under continual refinement and is available for download from GitHub. ASHLAR runs in Python and has no graphical user interface. Some fundamental knowledge of Python is therefore required for its use. Unlike Metamorph, ASHLAR can align several staining cycles of the same tissue based on a reference channel from each cycle. The data must be described by a .scan file and the reference channels must all be the same number (the default reference channel is 0). This feature makes ASHLAR suitable for multiplexing and background subtraction experiments. The output is a series of stitched TIFF files ready for analysis. ii. Determine the necessary parameters required to stitch the tiled images. Tiled images collected in Metamorph are listed in the reverse order from the ASHLAR default. Command line options (--flip-x and --flip-y) have been integrated into ASHLAR to correct for this. If there are sensor noise issues in the corners of tiles, this can be offset by applying a Gaussian filter (--filter-sigma SIGMA). It is recommended that you begin with a filter of 1 and increase as needed. When run from the home directory of a scanning project with multiple subdirectories containing image files, the following command line would stitch two cycles of staining in the same way, aligning by the default channel (0) and saving them to the subdirectory stitched: ashlar –flip-x –flip-y --filter-sigma 1 /c1/f/Scan 20x obj1.scan /c1/b/Scan 20x obj1.scan /c2/f/Scan 20x obj1.scan /c2/b/Scan 20x obj1.scan --o /stitched/ iii. steps.title: Prepare and Load Slides
steps.instruction: Prepare slides using mounting media (SlowFade Diamond or ProLong Glass) and clean with ammonia-free solution (e.g., Sparkle) to remove oils and debris. If multiplexing, secure the coverslip with VALAP.

substeps.instruction: Push slides tightly toward two edges of the holder and clamp them at both ends to ensure reproducible positioning for repeated scans.
Record the exact positions of the slides.

steps.title: Calibrate Stage and Focus
steps.instruction: Initialize the automated stage and set the Z-origin for the overview scan.

substeps.instruction: Move the stage to the measurable limits of the linear encoders and set this as (0,0).
Using a 5X objective, focus on tissue near the center of the TMA or multi-slide layout.
Set this position as 0 in the Z dimension (Device > Focus > Configure > Set Origin in Metamorph).

steps.title: Create Overview Image
steps.instruction: Generate a low-resolution map of the slide to identify tissue locations using the Metamorph Scan Slide module.

substeps.instruction: Load the '5X TMA Prelim Scan.scansetting' file.
Select the wavelength imaging, filter cube, and exposure time for a ubiquitous stain (e.g., Hoechst 33342).
Perform field-of-view calibration with the 5X objective to correct stage-camera alignment (target offset < 1 degree).
Define the rectangular scan region to include all tissues, extending corners slightly beyond the anticipated area.
Set the save folder (e.g., C:Data/user/YYMMDD/) and start the scan.
Verify the first column of tiles for correct exposure and alignment.

steps.title: Define and Align ROIs
steps.instruction: Manually select Regions of Interest (ROIs) on the overview scan and calibrate them for the high-power objective.

substeps.instruction: Switch to the high-power objective (e.g., 20X) and repeat the ScanSlide calibration to correct pixel dimensions.
Draw rectangular ROIs tightly around each tissue core in a logical sequence (e.g., top-down, left-right). Place tiny regions at empty positions to maintain numbering.
Save a reference map of the regions (Edit > Duplicate > As Displayed).

Correct ROI displacement caused by the objective change: send the stage to the center of an identifiable ROI, assess the location via the 20X objective, and use 'Region > Move all Regions' to adjust until aligned.
Save the final regions file (Regions > Save Regions).

steps.title: Configure Imaging Parameters
steps.instruction: Determine the Z-range and focal settings required for the automated high-resolution scan.

substeps.instruction: Determine the Z-range needed to find focus across all ROIs by checking focal points at the corners of the scan area.
Set the Z-origin at the midpoint of the determined focal limits (Device > Focus > Set origin).
In ScanSlide, configure the number of channels, filter cubes, exposures, and Z-offsets between channels.
Select a high-contrast signal (e.g., E-cadherin membrane stain) for the initial focal point.
Set the save file path and descriptive file name (e.g., Scan 20x obj1).
Save the scan settings in the image folder.

steps.title: Execute Automated Scan
steps.instruction: Run the master journal to acquire tiled images for each ROI.

substeps.instruction: Run the 'TMA Scanning Master.JNL' journal.
Select the focusing routine: '1-point' (center-based search) or '2-point' (averaging two points within 5 microns).
Choose the fine-focusing routine: built-in ScanSlide (every tile) or journal-programmed (user-defined intervals).
Load the Stage List Array file or allow the journal to create one from the ROI coordinates.
Input the Z-range (including a 10-micron buffer at both limits).
Input gross focus parameters: range, step size (default 3 microns), and threshold (determined via 'threshold finder.JNL').
Input fine focus parameters: range, step size, threshold, and frequency of checks.
Select the channels for gross and fine focusing.

steps.title: Review and Rescan
steps.instruction: Assess the quality of the acquired tiles and rescan any failed ROIs.

substeps.instruction: Copy the stage list array file to the image folder.
Open the .scan file for each ROI in ScanSlide to check for focus errors or incomplete imaging.
To rescan: load the preliminary scan and regions file, create a 'rescans' sub-folder, adjust the problematic ROIs, and manually focus before activating ScanSlide for those specific regions.
Copy the updated stage list array into the new save folder.

steps.title: Optional: Multiplexing or Background Subtraction
steps.instruction: Repeat the scanning process for additional markers or background subtraction using the original ROI map.

substeps.instruction: Clean and reload slides, ensuring they are positioned exactly as in the first scan.
Load previous scan settings, the preliminary scan, and the saved regions file.
Verify alignment by sending the stage to a known ROI and adjusting slide position (do not move the ROIs).
Run the scan journal, ensuring the reference channel is set to the ubiquitous stain for alignment.
Copy the stage list array and review scans as in Stage 4.

steps.title: Stitch Image Tiles
steps.instruction: Assemble individual tiles into composite images using a workstation.

substeps.instruction: Transfer data to a powerful offline computer.
Using Metamorph: Open the stage list array file, select 'Journal > Loop > Loop for all Images', and run 'Review TMA scans.JNL'.
Alternatively, use ASHLAR or the ImageJ Stitching plugin to create composite images (ASHLAR can output pyramidal TIFFs for OMERO).

description:
A DIY automated scanning microscope Page 2 of 30 Abstract: High-throughput, multiplex slide-scanning technologies have become widely-used. Advantages include the ability to archive digital copies of slides, review slides as teams using virtual microscope software, and standardize analytical approaches. One barrier to implementation is the cost of dedicated slide-
scanning devices. We describe a simple method that allows any microscope to be used for slide-scanning. The only requirements are that the microscope be equipped with a motorized filter turret (for multichannel fluorescence) and a motorized xyz stage. This example uses Metamorph, the most commonly used hardware-agnostic microscope control software. The approach can, however, be readily translated to open source applications as well as to dedicated control software provided by microscope manufacturers. The scripts, or journals, developed allow users to define multiple regions of interest and specific parameters, including ranges and channels used for focusing. Following acquisition, captured images can be stitched and displayed using open source virtual microscope software.
